questions.q: A front end calls the Task API with Authorization: Bearer <API key>, the key written into app.js. What is the real problem?
questions.explain: Anything shipped to the browser can be read in the developer tools. Browser apps prove who the user is with a login and a session (an HttpOnly cookie), not with a shared key.
options: The header name is wrong; it should be X-API-Key
Browsers refuse to send the Authorization header
Every visitor downloads app.js, so the key is public; a secret cannot live in browser code

questions.q: A request works with curl and from Node.js, but the same request from a page fails with a CORS error. Why?
questions.explain: The server answers every client the same way. Only the browser checks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers before letting page code read the response, because it acts for a user who may be logged in to many sites.
options: The server treats browsers differently from curl
CORS is enforced by the browser, to protect its user; curl and Node.js do not apply it
curl sends a secret header that browsers cannot send
The page must use XMLHttpRequest instead of fetch

questions.q: A page is served from https://tasks.example/app. Which request is same-origin?
questions.explain: An origin is scheme + host + port. Only the path may differ. A subdomain, plain HTTP or another port make it a different origin.

questions.q: What does the same-origin policy not prevent?
questions.explain: The policy blocks reading, not sending. That is why cross-site request forgery is possible and why cookies need SameSite and state-changing routes need CSRF protection.
options: A page reading the response of a fetch to another origin that has not allowed it
A page reading the DOM inside a frame from another origin
A page on another site making the browser send a form POST to your API, with the user's cookies (unless SameSite stops them)

questions.q: Which cross-origin request is sent without a preflight?
questions.explain: A simple request is one an HTML form or a plain link could have sent: GET, HEAD or POST, only safe headers, and a form content type. JSON bodies, other methods and custom headers need the server's permission first.

questions.q: The API answers Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, and the front end uses credentials: "include". What happens?
questions.explain: * is for public data that needs no user identity. For requests carrying cookies, the server must deliberately name each trusted origin.
options: The browser blocks the response: with credentials, the header must name the exact origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true must be present
The cookies are sent but the response body is empty
The browser downgrades to credentials: "omit" and retries

questions.q: To "fix CORS", a developer makes the server copy whatever Origin header arrives into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, with credentials allowed. What have they done?
questions.explain: Echoing any origin grants permission to every page on the internet. Compare the origin exactly against a configured allow-list, and echo it only when it matches.
options: Allowed every website to read logged-in users' data through their browsers

questions.q: Why does the API send Vary: Origin?
questions.explain: A shared cache that ignored the header could hand Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://tasks.example to a request from a different origin, or the reverse. Vary lists the request headers that change the answer.
options: It tells the browser to send the Origin header
The response depends on the Origin header, so caches must not reuse one origin's answer (with its CORS permission) for another origin
It hides the origin from the server logs

questions.q: Logged-in users get "Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check" on PATCH requests only. The server runs its session check before its CORS code. What is wrong?
questions.explain: The preflight asks for permission; it does not carry credentials. Answer it before authentication. That is why the lesson's API calls handleCors first.
options: Preflight OPTIONS requests never carry cookies, so the session check answers 401 before CORS can answer the preflight; CORS must run first
The server must allow the OPTIONS method in Access-Control-Allow-Methods

questions.q: What does HttpOnly on the session cookie protect against?
questions.explain: An HttpOnly cookie is invisible to document.cookie, so XSS cannot steal it. Secure handles plain HTTP, and SameSite handles cross-site requests.
options: The cookie being sent over plain HTTP
Other sites sending requests with the cookie
Page JavaScript, including an attacker's injected script, reading the session id and sending it elsewhere

questions.q: The front end on http://localhost:5173 logs in to the API on http://localhost:3000. Login succeeds, but every later request gets 401. The requests use fetch(url) with no options. What is missing?
questions.explain: With the default credentials: "same-origin", cookies from a cross-origin response are not stored and none are sent. The API must also allow credentials in its CORS headers.
options: credentials: "include", because the default only sends cookies to the page's own origin, and the API is a different origin
An Authorization header with the cookie's value
Nothing; the server must remember the user by IP address

questions.q: Why does a SameSite=Lax session cookie still work between app.tasks.example and api.tasks.example?
questions.explain: Origin compares scheme, host and port; site compares the registrable domain. CORS is about origins, SameSite about sites. Keeping the front end and the API on one site avoids third-party cookie problems.
options: They are different origins but the same site (the registrable domain tasks.example), and SameSite only restricts cross-site requests
It does not work; the cookie needs SameSite=None

questions.q: When does await fetch(url) give you the Response?
questions.explain: That is why there are two awaits: one for the headers, one for the body. You can check response.ok and the content type before deciding to read the body.
options: When the whole body has downloaded
As soon as the status and headers have arrived; the body is read afterwards with json(), text() or the stream
When the server closes the connection

questions.q: A page calls fetch(url, { headers: { Cookie: "session=abc" } }). What does the browser do with that header?
questions.explain: If pages could set Cookie, Origin or Host, they could impersonate users and other sites. The lesson's example showed these headers disappear from the Request.
options: Sends it, replacing the real cookies
Drops it silently: Cookie is a forbidden header that only the browser may set
Sends it only to same-origin URLs

questions.q: The API sends X-Total-Count: 57 on GET /tasks. The Network tab shows it, but cross-origin page code gets null from response.headers.get("x-total-count"). Why?
questions.explain: CORS controls headers as well as bodies. Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Total-Count makes it readable. Set-Cookie can never be exposed.
options: Cross-origin responses expose only a few safe headers to JavaScript; the server must list others in Access-Control-Expose-Headers
The header name must be written in capitals
Headers are only readable after the body has been read

questions.q: A developer "fixes" a CORS error by adding mode: "no-cors". What happens?
questions.explain: no-cors is for requests whose answer you do not need to read, like caching images. The fix for CORS errors is on the server (or serving both from one origin).
options: CORS is switched off and the JSON can be read
The request is sent, but the response is opaque: status 0, no headers, no readable body
The browser asks the user for permission
The request is sent through a proxy

questions.q: Why does the lesson's client show "Could not reach the server" when CORS blocks a request?
questions.explain: Browsers deliberately hide why a cross-origin request failed. A developer must read the console and the Network tab; the user can only be told to try again.
options: Because CORS errors always mean the server is down
Because page JavaScript receives the same TypeError for a CORS block as for a network failure; the reason is only in the developer console
Because the client ignores all errors

questions.q: A POST /orders times out. Why is retrying it automatically risky?
questions.explain: After a timeout you do not know what happened on the server. Retry idempotent requests freely; retry a POST only with an idempotency key the server uses to recognise duplicates.
options: Browsers forbid sending the same request twice
The server may have created the order and only the answer was lost, so a retry can create a second order
A timeout means the order definitely failed

questions.q: A search box sends a request per pause in typing, and sometimes shows results for an older term. What is the fix?
questions.explain: Responses can arrive in any order. Cancelling the old request means only the latest one can update the page. A longer debounce only makes the race rarer.
options: Abort the previous request with its AbortController when a new search starts, and ignore the resulting AbortError

questions.q: What is the simplest production setup that avoids CORS entirely?
questions.explain: Same-origin requests need no CORS headers and no preflights, and the default credentials setting sends the session cookie. Development servers offer a proxy setting for the same result locally.
options: Serving the front end and the API from one origin, with a reverse proxy sending /api/* to the API server
Putting the API key in the page

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Header names are case-insensitive, and Headers stores them in lower case, sorted. append adds another value to the same header, and get joins the values with a comma and a space.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A different host (even a subdomain) or port makes a different origin. Port 443 is the default for HTTPS, so writing it out changes nothing: the origin is still https://tasks.example.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A fetch with an already-aborted signal rejects straight away with an AbortError. A timeout signal aborts by itself, and its reason is a TimeoutError, so code can tell "the user cancelled" from "it took too long".

questions.q: This cookie parser has a bug. What does it print?
questions.explain: split("=") cuts at every =, and destructuring keeps only the first two pieces, so the value loses its trailing == (common in base64 ids). Split at the first = only: part.indexOf("=") and slice.

questions.q: Two searches run without cancelling. What does this print?
questions.explain: "rice" was asked for later but answered at about 20 ms; "ric" answered at 60 ms and overwrote it. The page shows results for a term the user is no longer searching for. Aborting the old request fixes it.
options:
answer for rice
answer for ric
page shows: ric

answer for ric
answer for rice
page shows: rice

answer for rice
answer for ric
page shows: rice

answer for ric
page shows: ric

questions.q: What Content-Type does fetch use when you give it a body but no header?
questions.explain: A string body is labelled plain text, even if it contains JSON, which is why the API answered 415 until the header was set. A URLSearchParams body is labelled as form data. Both are "simple" content types, so neither triggers a preflight.

questions.q: What does this error-message helper print?
questions.explain: The order of checks matters: a 401 from the login route means the password was wrong, anywhere else it means the session is gone. Server errors get a generic message (never the server's internals), and a missing body falls back to the status.
options:
Wrong email or password
Please log in again
Try again later
Request failed (404)

Please log in again
Please log in again
Try again later
Request failed (404)

Wrong email or password
Log in first
Try again later
undefined

Request failed (404)

questions.q: This server allows one origin. What does the Node.js script print? (It runs on your computer.)
questions.explain: The server answers both; only the allowed origin gets permission. A browser on the look-alike site would hide that response from its page, but Node.js, which applies no CORS rules, reads it anyway. Exact comparison with includes on an array rejects the look-alike; origin.startsWith("https://tasks.example") would have accepted it.

questions.q: Write needsPreflight(method, headers). A request is simple (no preflight) only if the method is GET, HEAD or POST, every header is one of accept, accept-language, content-language, content-type (any case), and a content-type, if present, is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain (ignore anything after ;).
questions.explain: The rule is "could an old HTML form have sent this?". Forms can send text/plain and URL-encoded bodies with GET or POST, so those need no permission; JSON, custom headers and other methods do.

questions.q: Write the browser's response check corsAllows(headers, origin, withCredentials). * is enough only without credentials. Otherwise access-control-allow-origin must equal origin, and with credentials access-control-allow-credentials must be "true".
questions.explain: Credentialed responses need two explicit signals from the server: the exact origin and the credentials flag. A missing header means no permission at all.

questions.q: Write parseCookieHeader(header) that turns a Cookie request header into an object. Split pairs on ;, trim them, and split each at the first = only, so values may contain =. Skip empty parts.
questions.explain: Cookie values are often base64, which ends in =. indexOf plus slice splits at the first = and keeps the rest intact. Headers are client input, so the parser must survive empty and malformed parts.

questions.q: Write isAllowedOrigin(origin, allowList) for a CORS middleware. It returns true only when origin is a string exactly equal to an entry in the list. Look-alike domains, other schemes, ports, and the literal origin "null" (sent by sandboxed pages and local files) must be refused.
questions.explain: Exact comparison against a list is the only safe test. startsWith, endsWith or an unanchored regular expression accept look-alikes. Never put "null" on an allow-list: any sandboxed iframe can send it.
questions.expected:
https://tasks.example true
https://tasks.example.evil.com false
http://tasks.example false
http://localhost:5174 false
null false
undefined false

questions.q: Without AbortController, you can still ignore stale answers. Write latestOnly(fn): it returns an async wrapper that calls fn(...args), and resolves with the result only if no newer call was started in the meantime; a stale call resolves with undefined.
questions.explain: Each call takes a number from a counter in the closure. When an answer arrives, it is used only if its number is still the latest. Aborting is better when you can, because it also stops the network work; this pattern works for any async function.

questions.q: Write fetchTasks(api, ms) that calls api({ signal }) with AbortSignal.timeout(ms) and returns the result, or the string "timed out" if the signal's TimeoutError ends it. The fake API respects the signal like fetch does.
questions.explain: AbortSignal.timeout aborts with a TimeoutError, which the code recognises by name. Any other error is re-thrown, so real failures are not mistaken for slowness.

questions.q: Write sessionCookie(id, { maxAgeSeconds }) that builds the Set-Cookie value for a session with safe defaults: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/ and Max-Age. Refuse an id that is not 64 lower-case hex characters by throwing new Error("bad session id").
questions.explain: Building headers from values means validating them: a value containing ; could add its own attributes to the cookie. Max-Age=0 is how logout deletes the cookie.
questions.expected:
session=aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600
session=0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=0
bad session id

questions.q: The API answers a successful login with 204 No Content. What does this print?
questions.explain: An empty body is not valid JSON, so json() rejects. That is why the lesson's client checks for 204 before reading the body. As text, the empty body is simply "".

questions.explain: A combined signal aborts as soon as any of its inputs does, and takes that input's reason. So one request can stop when the user cancels or when it takes too long, and the reason says which.

questions.q: Write a simplified sameSite(a, b): two URLs are the same site when their schemes match and the last two labels of their host names match (app.tasks.example → tasks.example). Ports do not matter. (Real browsers use the Public Suffix List, so that a.co.uk and b.co.uk are different sites.)
questions.explain: These are different origins in every case, but the first two pairs are the same site, so a SameSite=Lax cookie flows between them. A different registrable domain, or plain HTTP against HTTPS, is a different site.
